METHODS  OF  DETERMINATION  OF 

THE  CHEMICAL  COMPOSITION  OF  ASH 

OF  COAL  AND  COKE

AMENDMENT  NO.    1     NOVEMBER  2002 

TO 

IS  1355:1984    METHODS  OF  DETERMINATION  OF 

THE  CHEMICAL  COMPOSITION  OF  ASH  OF 

COAL  AND  COKE 

(  First  Revision  ) 

(  Page  29,  clause  6.16 )  —  Insert  the  following  new  clauses  after  6.16: 

6.16.0  General  —  Two  methods  (Method  A  and  Method  B)  have  been 
prescribed  for  the  determination  of  alkalis. 

6.16.1  Method  A 

(  Pages  29  to  31,  clauses  6.16.1  to  6.16.10  )  —  Renumber  these  clauses  as 
6.16.1.1  to  6.16.1.10  and  insert  the  following  new  clauses  after  6.16.1.10: 

6.16.2  Method  B 

6.16.2.1  General 

Determination  of  alkalis  by  this  method  shall  be  carried  out  using  flame 
photometer. 

6.16*2.2  Terminology 

a)  Ash  —  Inorganic  residue  left  when  powdered  coal  or  coke  is 
incinerated  in  air  to  constant  mass  at  800  ±  iS^C. 

b)  Ash  so  determined  is  not  the  same  as  the  original  mineral  matter 
associated  with  the  coal,  because  changes  take  place  during 
incineration,  namely,  the  loss  of  combined  water  and  carbon  dioxide 
from  carbonates,  etc. 

6.16.23  Purity  of  reagents 

Analytical  grade  reagents  shall  be  used.  Unless  otherwise  indicated  all  reagents 
to  be  of  high  purity  to  permit  its  use  without  lessening  the  accuracy  of  the 
determination.  Water  to  be  used  shall  be  doubled  distilled  and  free  from  Na**^  <m* 
K"^  radicals. 

Price  Group  2 


Amend  No.  Ito  IS  1355  :  1984 

6.16.2.4  Preparation  of  coal/coke  ash 

Prepare  3  to  5  g  of  ash  from  thoroughly  mixed  air  dried  coal  or  coke  which  has 
been  ground  to  pass  212  micron  sieve.  Spread  the  coal  or  coke  in  a  layer  not  over 
6  mm  in  depth  in  a  fireclay  or  porcelain  roasting  dish.  Place  in  a  cold  muffle 
furnace  and  heal  gradually  to  the  temperature  500  C  in  one  hour  and  800  ±  15^C 
in  two  hours.  Allow  the  ash  to  cool,  transfer,  agate  and  store  for  analysis. 
Thoroughly  mix  each  sample  before  weighing.  If  stored,  reignite  before 
weighing.  If  difficulty  in  ashing  is  encountered  for  coke,  may  be  ignited  at 
^OOtSO^'C. 

6.16.2.5  Apparatus 

a)  Balance  —  sensitive  to  0. 1  mg 

b)  Crucible  —  platinum  basins,  100-ml  capacity,  shall  be  used  for 
decomposition  of  the  ash  with  HF. 

c)  Flame  Photometer 

d)  Muffle  Furnace  —  Electrically-heated  muffle  furnace  with  good  air 
circulation  and  capable  of  maintaining  a  temperature  of  approximately 
lOOO'^C. 

6.16.2.6  Preparation  analysis  solutions  (standard  and  blank) 

a)  Reagents 

1 )  Hydrochloric  acid  (specific  gravity  1.18)  concentrated  HCl 

2)  Hydrofluoric  acid  (specific  gravity  1.15)  concentrated  HF 

3)  Perchloric  acid  (about  70  percent,  specific  gravity  1 .67)  HCIO4 

b)  Preparation  of  Stock  Solution 

1)  Potassium,  concentrated  stock  solution  (100  ppm)  —  Dissolve 
0. 190  70  g  of  KCl  /  0.258  6  g  of  KNO3  or  0.222  8  g  of  K2SO4  in 
water  and  dilute  to  l(X)0  cm  . 

2)  Sodium  concentrated  stock  solution  (100  ppm)  —  Dissolve  0.25 1  6  g 
of  NaCl  /  0308  8  g  of  Na2S04  in  water  and  dilute  to  1  000  cm^ 


Amend  No.  1  to  IS  1355:  1984 

c)  Preparation  of  synthetic  ash  solution 

1)  Dissolve  1.0  g  of  aluminium  in  10  cm    ot  H2SO4  and   add  100 
cm"  of  water; 

2)  Dissolve  2.0  g  of  iron  in  10  cm^  of  H2SO4  ( I  :  1 )  and  add  100  cm-^ 
of  water; 

3)  Dissolve  1.25  g  of  CaC03  in  3  cm'^  of  H2SO4  (1  :  1)  and  about 
6  000  cm  of  water  is  added  to  it;  and 

4)  Dissolve  1  g  of  magnesium  sulphate  (MgS04)in  water.  Combine 
all  solution,  filter  and  dilute  to  1  000  cm  . 

d)  Preparation  of  standard  solution  —  To  prepare  different  ppm  level 
(10,  20,  40  or  I)  standard  solution  of  sodium  and  potassium,  pipette 
(10, 20, 40  or  1)  ppm  of  sodium  or  potassium  from  stock  solution  into  a 
1(X)  cm  volumetric  flask.  Add  10  cm  of  synthetic  ash  solution  and 
10  cm  of  sodium  or  potassium  (i.e.  if  sodium  standard  is  prepared,  add 
10  cm  of  potassium  stock  solution  or  vice  versa)  dilute  with  water  to 
the  mark  and  mix,  store  in  plastic  bottle. 

6.16.2.7  Dissolution  of  sample 

To  dissolve,  grind  a  representative  sample  of  ash  to  pass  through  100  mesh  sieve 
and  remix  thoroughly.  Place  0.1  g  of  sample  in  a  100  cm  platinum  basin,  add 
5  cm*^  of  HF  3  cm*^  of  HNO3  and  2  cm"^  HCIO4  and  digested  to  dryness.  Repeat 
the  process.  Once  dried  add  2  cm  of  HCIO4  and  evaporate  to  dryness.  Add  few 
drops  of  HCIO4  or  HCI  to  moisten  the  mass  and  add  20  ml  distilled  water  and 
evaporate  the  same  to  1/2  of  its  volume.  Transfer  the  same  solution  by  filtering 
and  make  the  volume  to  250  ml  in  a  volumetric  flask.  Take  aliquot  solution  to 
aspirate  for  determination  of  alkalies. 

6.16.2.8  Calibration 

After  adjusting  the  flame  spectrophotometer  according  to  the  manufacturer's 
direction,  set  the  wave  length  to  589  nm  and  aspirate  sodium  solution  of  different 
ppm  level  and  determine  the  transmittance  reading.  Repeat  this  operation  for 
checking  the  transmittance.  Test  the  blank  solution  and  make  similar 
measurements  for  the  standard  potassium  solution  at  a  wave  length  of  766  nm 
and  plot  the  data  obtained. 


Amend  No.  1  to  IS  13SS  :  1984 

6.16«2.9  Determination  of  Alkalies 

a)  Set  the  instrument  as  has  been  done  while  calibration.  Rinse  a  sample 
cup  with  the  solution  it  is  to  contain  and  fill  separate  cups  with  standard 
solution  of  required  ppm  level.  Adjust  instrument  according  to  the 
range  of  standard.  Make  the  readings  of  sample  solution  and  blank 
solution.  Subtract  the  blank  reading  from  the  sample  readings  and 
determine  the  concentration  of  sodium  and  potassium  in  the  test 
solution  from  the  appropriate  working  curve. 

b)  Calculation 

Calculate  the  percent  sodium  oxide  and  potassium  oxide  as  follows: 

1)  Sodium  oxide  (NaiO),  percent  =  Xnh  x  0.337  5 

Where  XNa    =  ppm  sodium  when  0.1  g  of  sample  in  250  cm 
solution  taken. 

If  XNa  =  1  ppm,  then  the  sodium  oxide  percent  contained  in  250 
cm  which  originally  came  from  0. 1  g  ash  is  0.000  337  5  g,  that  is, 
0.337  percent 

2)  Potassium  oxide  (K2O),  percent  =  Xk  x  0,  301  25 

Where  Xk  =  ppm  potassium  when  0. 1  g  of  sample  taken  in  250  cm 
solution. 

If  Xk  "=  1  ppm,  then  the  potassium  oxide  percent  contained  in  250  ml 
which  originally  came  from  0.1  g  ash  is  0.000  301  25  g,  that  is, 
0.301  percent. 

6.16.2.10  Conversion  calculation  from  ppm  to  percentage  (100  unit  in  digital 
display  is  equivalent  to  10  ppm) 

a)    4Na  +  O2  =  2  NaiO,  that  is,  Na  =  Vi  NaaO 

Hence  conversion  factor  from  Na  to  Na20  is  1.35 


So,  ppm  to  percent  conversion  is: 

If  Xppm  ==  experimental  value  i 

Xppmx  1.35  X  1/0.1  X  1/10^  x 

0. 1  g  sample  is  taken  and  volume  made  up  to  250  ml) 


If  Xppm  ==  experimental  value  after  deduction  of  blank  value,  then 
Xppm  X  1.35  X  1/0.1  X  1/10^  x  100  x  250  =  Xppm  x  0.337  5  (when 


Amend  No.  1  to  IS  1355  :  1984 

b)    4K  +  02  =  2K20 
K  =  1/2  K:0 
Ucncc  conversion  factor  from  K  lo  K2O  is  1.205 
So,  ppm  10  percent  conversion: 

If  Xppm  ==  experimental  value  after  deduction  of  blank  value,  then 
Xppm  X  1.205  X  1/0.1  x  1/10^  x  100  x  250  =  Xppm  x  0.301  5  (v^hen 
0. 1  g  sample  is  taken  and  volume  made  up  to  250  ml) 

NOTE  —  The  method  is  applicable  for  total  NaiO,  K2O  content.  It  shall  also  be  applied 
to  both  water  soluble,  as  well  as  acid  soluble  alkalis. 

a)  Water  Soluble  Alkali  —  After  suitable  extraction  with  water,  the  extract  after 
filtration  and  marking  volume  250  ml,  the  same  procedure  may  be  adopted  for  the 
said  solution 

b)  Acid  Soluble  Alkali  —  After  suitable  extraction  with  desired  acid,  the  extract  after 
filtration  and  making  volume  250  ml,  the  same  procedure  may  be  adopted  for  the 
said  solution.

IS  1 1355  -  1984 

Indian  Standard 

METHODS  OF  DETERMINATION  OF 
THE  CHEMICAL  COMPOSITION  OF  ASH 
OF  COAL  AND  COKE 

(  First  Revision  J 

0.    FOREWORD 

0.1  This  Indian  Standard  (  First  Revision  )  was  a  dopted  by  the  Indiau 
Standards  Institution  on  7  March  1984,  after  the  draft  finalized  by  the  Solid 
Mineral  Fuels  Sectional  Committee  had  been  approved  by  the  Petroleum, 
Coal  and  Related  Products  Division  Council. 

0.2  This  standard  was  published  as  methods  of  test  for  ash  of  coal  ano 
coke  in  the  year  1959  when  the  country  did  not  possess  much  systematic 
data  of  analysis  of  her  coal  and  coke  by  uniform  and  standard  methods  to 
prescribe  its  own  methods  of  test.  This  standard  at  that  time  provided 
basis  for  further  investigational  work.  The  committee  responsible  for  the 
preparation  of  this  standard  decided  to  revise  it  in  the  light  of  the  past 
experience  and  latest  development  in  the  field. 

0.3  In  this  revised  standard  the  title  has  been  modified  to  emphasize 
that  it  deals  with  the  methods  of  determination  of  only  chemical 
composition  of  ash  of  coal  and  coke  and  therefore  the  clause  dealing 
with  fusibility  of  ash  has  been  excluded.  The  Committee  at  the  time  of 
preparation  of  this  standard  took  cognizance  of  the  fact  that  for  ash  fusion 
characteristics,  preparation  of  a  separate  standard  may  be  taken  up 
subsequently  when  more  data  is  available  on  the  basis  of  sophisticated 
equipment  such  as  Lcitz  Heating  Microscope  or  atomic  absorption, 
spectrophotometer,  etc. 

0.4  The  Committee  has  separately  formulated  an  Indian  Standard 
IS  :  5069  (  Part  2  )-1969*  to  prescribe  methods  of  determination  of  ash  in 
brown  coal  and  lignites. 

0.5  In  the  preparation  of  this  standard  considerable  assistance  has  been 
derived  from  ISO  1171-1981  'Solid  mineral  fuels  determination  ofash\ 
issued  by  the  International  Organization  for  Standardization  (  ISO  ). 

0.6  For  the  purpose  of  deciding  whether  a  particular  requirement  of  this 
standard  is  complied  with,  the  final  value,  observed  or  calculated,  cxprcsrin. 

■^Methods  of  test  for  brown  coals  and  lignites  :  Part  2  Determination  of  ash. 


IS  1 1355  -  1984 

the  result  of  a  test  or  analVsis.  shall  be  rounded  off  in  accordance  with 
IS  :  2-1960*.  The  number  of  significant  places  retained  in  the  rounded 
off  value  should  be  the  same  as  that  of  the  specified  value  in  this  standard. 


1.  SCOPE 

1.1  This  standard  prescribes  the  methods  of  test  for  the  analysis  of  ash  of 
coal  and  coke.  The  standard  contains  definitions  of  terms  and  methods 
of  preparation  of  ash. 

1.2  Should  any  inconsistency  exist  between  the  requirements  of  this 
standard  and  those,  if  any,  given  in  standards  for  individual  materials, 
the  latter  shall  prevail. 

1.3  Test  methods  not  described  in  this  standard,  and  not  specified  in  the 
standard  for  individual  materials  shall  be  subject  to  agreement  between 
the  purchaser  and  the  vendor. 

2.  TERMINOLOGY 

2.0  For  the  purpose  of  this  standard  the  following  definitions  shall  apply. 

2.1  Ash— Inorganic  residue  left  when  powdered  coal  or  coke  is  incinerated 
in  air  to  constant  mass  under  specified  conditions. 

2.1.1  Ash  as  determined  is  not  the  same  as  the  original  mineial  matter 
associated  with  the  coal,  because  changes  take  place  during  incineration, 
namely  the  loss  of  combined  water,  or  carbon  dioxide  from  carbonates, 
etc.  Recommended  formulae  for  the  calculation  of  mineral  matter  in  coal 
from  ash  arc  given  under  6  of  IS  :  4311-1967t. 

3.  QUALITY  OF  REAGENT 

3.1  Unless  specified  otherwise,  pure  chemicals  ( see  Note )  shall  be 
employed  and  distilled  water,  conforming  to  IS  :  1070-1977t  shall  be  used 
where  the  use  of  water  as  a  reagent  is  specified. 

Note  —  'Pure    chemicals'    shall  mean  chemicals  that  do  not  contain  impurities 
which  affect  results  of  analysis. 

4.  SAMPLING 

4.1  Methods  of  Sampling  -—  Methods  of  sampling  shall  be  as  prescribed 
in  IS  :  436  (  Part  1  /  Section  1  )  -  1964§  and  IS  :  436  (  Part  1  /  Section  2  )  - 
197611  for  coal  and  IS  :  436  (  Part  2  )  -  196511  for  coke. 

*Rules  for  rounding  off  numerical  values  (  revised ). 

tMcthods  for  the  determination  of  mineral  matter  in  coal. 

I  Water  for  general  laboratory  use  (  second  revision  ). 

^Methods  for  sampling  of  coal  and  coke:  Part  1   Sampling  of  coal,  Section  1  Manual 
sampling. 

I'Methods    for  sampling  of  coal  and  coke:  Part    1   Sampling  of  coal,  Section  2 
Mechanical  sampling.

4.2  PreparatioD  of  Samples  for  Test 


4.2.0  General  —  Methods  of  sampling  prescribed  in  4.1  shall  have 
been  followed  in  the  preparation  of  samples  of  coal  and  coke  sent  to  the 
laboratory. 

4.2.1  The  analysis  sample  prepared  in  accordance  with  4.1  shall 
consist  of  0*5  kg  of  air-dried  coal  or  coke  ground  to  pass  IS  sieve  20. 

4.2.2  The  percentage  loss  of  moisture  in  air-drying  shall  be  required 
to  be  recorded  on  the  label  together  with  the  method  of  sampling  used. 

4.2.3  Samples  which  are  received  in  the  laboratory  already  ground 
to  pass  IS  sieve  20  (212  microns  )  shall  be  re-sieved  to  verify  that  all 
the  material  passes  this  seive,  and  then  air-dried  for  24  hours  and 
mixed  and  bottled  as  above.  Should  a  sample  of  coai  or  coke  be  trans- 
ported to  any  distance  between  the  point  of  prepaiation  and  the 
laboratory  under  conditions  in  which  it  may  be  shaken  down  and  may 
cause  segregation  to  any  degree,  the  entire  contents  of  the  bottle  shall  be 
re-mixed  before  analytical  work  is  started.  The  use  of  mechanical  devices 
is  recommended. 

4.2.4  The  normal  method  of  mixing  coal  or  coke  in  the  laboratory 
is  to  roll  it  on  a  sheet  of  rubber  cloth,  and  to  turn  it  over  at  intervals 
with  a  large  spatulla  or  flat  spoon.  This  method  is  not  entirely  satisfactory, 
since  the  movement  of  the  coal  tends  \o  cause  segregation.  The 
difficulty  may  be  overcome  in  part  by  spreading  the  mixed  sample 
in  a  thin  layer  and  filling  the  analysis  bottle  by  means  of  small  mcrements 
taken  with  the  spoon  from  spaces  spaced  uniformly  over  the  surface 
of  the  layer.  This  method  of  filling  is  particularly  necessary  when  more 
than  one  bottle  is  being  filled.  A  laboratory  mechanical  mixer  is,  however, 
preferable. 

4.2.5  In  case  an  analysis  sample  ground  to  pass  IS  sieve  20(211 
micron  )  is  not  received  in  the  laboratory,  a  sample  of  air-dried  material 
shall  be  prepared  from  th^  sample  of  coal  or  coke  received  in  the 
laboratory  in  the  manner  prescribed  under  6.3.2  of  IS:  1350  (  Part  I  )  - 
1969*  and  the  loss  of  moisture  on  air-drying  recorded.

5-  GENERAL 

5.1  Ash  —  As  prcpa'-cd  in  the  laboratory  by  the  incineration  of  powdered 
coal  or  coke  in  an  oxidizing  atmosphere.  It  consists  mainly  of  oxides  of 
silicon,  aluminium,  iron,  calcium,  mai;ncsium  and  sulphur,  with  smaller 
amounts  of  the  alkalis,  a  d  the  oxides  of  titanium,  manganese,  phos- 
phorus and  arsenic.  Some  of  the  oxides  are  present  in  the  free  state  and 
others  are  combined  to  form  silicates,  su'phates,  phosphates  and 
arsenates.  The  recognized  analytical  methods  for  the  quantitative  analysis 
of  mixtures  of  inorganic  oxides  ari^  applicable  also  to  the  constituents 
of  coal  ash  and  cock  ash  The  scheme  of  analysis  for  coa' and  coke 
ashes  is,  however,  considerably  simpler  than  schemes  for  the  analysis 
of  silicate  minerals  in  general.  For  example,  the  first  two  analytical 
groups  are  not  included  and  only  one  separation  of  group  members  is 
necessary,  namely,  for  sodium  and  potassium. 

5.2  Ash  prepared  from  a  coke  usrally  represents,  in  ultimate  composi- 
tion the  ash  from  the  corresponding  coal,  the  main  point  of  difference 
being  the  presence  of  more  of  sulphate  in  coke  ash. 

5.3  The  main  analysis  which  consists  of  the  determination  of  silicon, 
barium,  iron,  aluminium,  titanium,  calcium  and  magnesium  can  be 
carried  out  on  one  portion  of  ash  as  described  under  6.1  to  6.13. 
Determination  of  manganese,  phosj  horous,  the  alkalis  and  sulphur, 
when  required,  are  carried  out  on  separate  portions  of  ash  as  described 
under  6.14  to  6.17. 

5.4  Preparation  of  Ash  for  Analysis  —  (  see  also  6.3  and  6.4  ) 

5.4.1  Ash  prepared  in  different  ways  from  the  same  coal  may  differ 
appreciably  in  composition.  For  example,  coal  incinerated  at  a  dull- red 
heat  may  give  an  ash  containing  cabonates  which  would  be  decomposed 
quantitatively  at  higher  temperatures.  Again,  when  thick  layers  of 
powdered  coal  arc  incinerated,  reducing  conditions  bring  about  the 
formation  of  sulphides  which  are  oxidized  only  with  difficulty  ;  also,  a 
greater  amount  of  sulphur  may  be  retained  in  the  ash  than  is  the  case 
when  the  coal  is  incinerated  in  thin  layers. 

5.4.2  The  conditions  specified  for  the  determination  of  the  ash  content 
of  coal  or  coke  [see  8.2  of  IS:  1350  (Part  1).  1 969*]  ensure  the  repro- 
ducibility of  results  in  different  laboratories.  Thin  layers  of  coal  or  coke 
arc  incinerated  at  815  ±  lO^C,  in  an  oxidizing  atmosphere  until  the 
residue  is  constant  in  mass.  Under  these  conditions  of  preparation, 
the  ash  should  be  free  from  carbonates  and  from  all  but  small  traces  of 
sulphide,  but  all  the  iron  compounds  should  be  fully  oxidized.    When 


^Methods  of  test  for  coal  and  coke  :  Part  1  Proximate  analysis  (first  revision  ). 


IS  :  1355  -  1984 

thft  method  is  used,  however,  for  the  preparation  of  an    appreciable 
quantity  of  ash  for  analysis  it  is  tedious,  extremely  so  with  low-ash  fuels. 

5.4.3  This  tedium  may  be  avoided  by  the  preparation  of  two  separate 
samples  of  ash  for  analysis,  if  certain  precautions  are  observed.  The 
separate  samples  are  referred  to  as  standard  ash  and  hulk  ash  : 

a)  Prepare  the  standard  ash  in  the  standard  manner  [  see  8.2  of 
IS  :  1350  (  Part  1)-1969*  ]  and  determine  the  moisture  and  ash 
contents  of  the  fuel  during  the  preparation.  Use  the  standard 
ash  for  the  determination  of  sulphur  in  the  ash. 

b)  Prepare  the  bulk  ash  by  any  non-standard  method.  Ascertain  the 
moisture  contents  of  the  fuel  and  determine  the  ash  contrnt, 
as  prepared  by  the  non-standard  method. 

c)  Correct  all  analytical  results  obtained  on  the  hulk  ash  to  ti.c 
standard  ash  basis ;  the  presence  of  carbonates  or  sulphid'.:., 
if  any,  in  the  ash  prepared  by  the  non-standard  method  beinj 
ignored.  The  results  shall  be  multiplied  by  the  fraction  given 
below: 

Percentage  of  hulk  ash  on  the  dry-fuel  basis 
Percentage  of  standard  ash  on  the  dry-fuel  basis 

5.5  General  Precautions  and  Instructions 

5.5.1  Good-quality  apparatus,  particularly  glassware,  is  an  essential 
requirement  for  the  accurate  analysis  of  ash.  If  porcelain  dishes  arc 
used  where  platinum  is  not  available,  they  should  be  kept  specially  for 
this  purpose  and  care  should  be  taken  to  ensure  that  the  glaze  is 
undamaged.  All  reduction  in  particle  size  of  the  ash  should  be  carried 
out  in  an  agate  mortar. 

5.5.2  Desiccators  should  be  recharged  frequently  with  the  desiccating 
agent.  Ignited  residues,  which  often  act  as  dehydrating  agents,  should 
not  be  allowed  to  remain  in  desiccators  before  weighing  for  longer  periods 
than  are  necessary  for  cooling.  Usually  a  period  of  15  to  30  minutes  is 
sufficient. 

5.5.3  Special  attention  is  called  to  the  care  necessary  in  any  operations 
involving  the  use  of  perchloric  acid.  This  acid,  particularly  when  over 
70  percent  in  strength,  or  when  hot,  combines  with  organic  matter  or 
easily-oxidizable  inorganic  matter,  sufficiently  violently  to   lead   to   serious 


^Method  of  test  for  coal  and  coke  :  Part  I  Proximate  analysis  ( first  revision  ). 


IS  1 1355  - 1984 

explosions.  Explosions  may  also  be  caused  by  the  vapours  of  the  heated 
acid.  Great  care,  therefore,  should  be  taken  to  avoid  the  contact  of 
this  acid  with  grease,  dust,  coke  or  rubber  stoppers,  etc,  and  to  ensure 
that  all  apparams  used  in  operations  involving  pcrrchloric  acid  is  scrupuiously 
clean.    This  applies  particularly  to  the  lip  of  acid  storage  bottle. 

5.5.4  All  reagents  used  should  be  of  the  highest  purity  obtainable  ;  in 
this  respect,  particular  attention  should  be  given  to  the  ammonium 
hydroxide.  Reference  to  Vater'  means  distilled  water,  which  should  be  free 
from  dissolved  gases. 

5.5.5  When  ash  analysis  is  being  undertaken  for  the  first  time,  duplicate 
blank  determinations  should  be  carried  out  with  all  methods,  using  the 
same  reagents  and  laboratory  conditions  as  in  the  actual  analysis.;  the 
results  obtained  should  be  appllied  as  corrections  to  the  ash  analysis. 
When  new  stocks  of  reagents  are  obtained  or  laboratory  conditions  change, 
new  blank  determinations  .should  be  carried  out.  Until  operators  are  well 
trained  in  the  technique  of  ash  analysis,  it  is  advisable  to  carry  out 
duplicate  analysis  on  each  sample. 

5.6  Methods  —  Two  schemes  of  analysis  and  procedures  are  described. 
Of  these,  the  scheme  and  proceduies  described  under  Tare  quicker  and 
may  be  adopted  where  applicable.  In  case  of  dispute,  the  scheme  and 
procedure  prescribed  under  6  shall  be  adopted  for  referee  purposes.

6.1.1  Shallow  Silica  Dishes  —  5  cm  in  diameter  and  1  cm  deep.

6.1.3  Platinum  Crucible  —  about  30  ml  in  capacity. 

6.1.4  Hot  Air  Bath  —  illustrated  in  Fig.  1.  It  is  constructed  of  sheet 
iron  the  base  being  welded  to  the  sides.  Nichrome  wire  is  suitable  to 
support  the  crucblc  pnnided  it  has  been  heated  initially  to  dull-red 
heat  to  prevent  possible  staining  of  the  crucible.  In  use,  the  bath  is 
supported  bv  resting  the  loose  metal  flange  on  a  tripod  stand  and  the 
base  is  heated  to  just  below  dull-redness. 

6.1.5  Platinum  Basin  —  about  150  ml  in  capacity.

6.2.12  Concentrated  Ammonium  Hydroxide   Solution  —  sp  gr  0*90. 

6.2.12.1  Bench  bottles  of  ammonium  hydroxide  often  contain  appre- 
ciable quantities  of  impurities,  usually  silica  and  ammonium  carbonate, 
the  former  being  a  result  of  attack  on  the  glass  and  the  latter  arising  from 
unnecessary  exposure  to  air.  Contamination  by  these  two  impurities  can 
be  avoided  by  purchasing  pure  reagent,  storing  it  in  waxed  bottles,  and 
talcing  care  to  replace  stoppers  promptly  after  use. 

6.2.13  Dilute  Ammonium  Hydroxide  Solution  —  one  volume  of 
concentrated  ammonium  hydroxide  solution  diluted  with  nine  volumes  of 
water.

6.2.21.1  Standardization  — Take  25  ml  of  a  decinormal  solution  of 
ferrous  ammonium  sulpnaie,  add  20  ml  of  dilute  sulphuric  acid  and  cool 
to  about  IOC.  Add  potassium  permanganate  solution  until  the  iron  is 
oxidized  and  there  is  so  small  an  excess  of  permanganate  that  the  pink 
colour  fados  away  quickly.  Add  15  ml  of  ammonium  thiocyanate  solution 
and  allow  the  liquid  to  attain  room  temperature.  Titrate  with  a  solution 
of  mercurous  nitrate,  shaking  vigorously  throughout  the  nitration,  until 
the  colour  of  ferric  thiocyanate  is  just  discharged.

acid  ),  standardized  against  potassium  permanganate  solution  (  see  6.2.19  ).

6.2.36  Standard  Nitric  Acid  —  approximately  01  N  obtained  by  dilrting 
64  ml  of  concentrated  nitiic  acid  with  >Aater  to  one  litre  and  standardizing

6.2.38  Ammonium  Molybdate  Solution  —  Dissolve  100  g  of  pure  molybdic 
acid  (  containing  not  less  than  85  percent  of  MoO. )  in  a  mixture  of  400  ml 
cold  water  and  80  ml  of  concentrated  ammonium  hydroxide  solution.  Mix 
the  solution  by  shaking  and  pour  slowly  into  a  solution  of  400  ml  of 
concentrated  nitric  acid  in  600  ml  of  water,  contained  in  a  flask.  Mix  by 
shaking  during  the  addition.  Add  to  the  mixture  about  0*05  g  of 
microcosmic  salt  [  Na  (NH4)  HPO4,  4HaO  ],  dissolved  in  a  small  quantity 
of  water.  Heat  the  mixture  gently  to  65°C,  shaking  frequently.  Allow  the 
solution  to  cool,  and  leave  it  to  stand  overnight,  then  decant  the  clear 
supernatant  liquid  into  a  dark-brown  stoppered  bottle.  Do  not  keep  the 
reagent  longer  than  two  months. 

6.2.39  Potassium  Nitrate  Solution  —  neutral,  containing  one  gram  of 
KNO,  per  litre. 

6.2.40  Standard  Sodium  Hydroxide  Solution  —  approximately  O'l  N,  in 
water,  standardized  against  decinormal  nitric  acid  stored  in  an  atmosphere 
free  from  carbon  dioxide. 

6.2.41  Phenolphthalein  Indicator,  Neutral  —  Containing  0'5  g  of 
phenolphthalein  dissolved  in  100  ml  of  95  percent  rectified  spirit  ( conforming 
to  IS  :  323-1959*  )  and  add  a  dilute  solution  of  sodium  hydroxide  drop  by 
drop  until  the  colour  turns  faint  pink. 

6.2.42  Ammonium  Chloride  —  solid,  free  from  alkalis  as  far  as  possible. 

6.2.43  Calcium  Carbonate  —  precipitated,  free  from  alkalis  as  far  as 
possible. 

6.2.44  Concentrated  Barium  Chloride  Solution  —  containing  100  |  of 
BaCl,.  2H,0  per  litre. 

6.2.45  Dilute  Barium  Chloride  Solution  —  one  volume  of  concentrated 
barium  chloride  solution  diluted  to  ten  volumes  with  water.

6.3  Determination  of  Ash  Content  and  Preparation  of  Standard  Ash  for 
Determination  of  Sulphur  —  Accurately  weigh  into  the  shallow  silica  dish, 
TOO  to  rOl  g  of  coal  or  coke  of  known  moisture  content  and  ground  to 
pass  IS  Sieve  20  (  211  microns).  Place  it  in  a  muffle  furnace  at  room 
temperature,  and  raise  the  temperature  to  500  ±  15°C  in  30  minutes. 
Maintain  at  this  temperature  for  30  minutes  and  then  heat  in  an  oxidizing 
atmosphere  at  815  ±  10"C  for  one  hour,  or  until  constant  in  mass.  After 
incineration  cover  the  dish  and  transfer  the  covered  dish  to  a  desiccator 
and  allow  to  cool  by  the  side  of  the  balance.  When  cool,  weigh  the  dish, 
brush  out  the  ash  into  a  beaker  ready  for  the  determination  oC  sulphur  (  see 
6.17  )  and  rcwcigh  the  empty  dish.  Obtain  the  mass  of  ash  by  difference 
and  note  the  result  as  a  percentage  of  coal  and  coke.  Repeat  the  deter- 
mination until  a  sufficient  quantity  (  10  g )  of  ash  has  been  prepared. 

6.4  Preparttion  of  Bulk  Ash  for  General  Ash  Analysis  —  Weigh,  to  the 
nearest  0*01  g,  sufficient  coal  or  coke,  of  known  moisture  content,  to  yield 
enough  ash  for  the  main  analysis.  Transfer  to  silica  basins.  Arrange  the 
sample  in  small  heaps  and  ignite  it  in  the  open  with  a  flame  or  in  a  muflUe 
furnace.  Allow  the  heaps  to  smoulder  for  a  few  hours  to  destroy  any 
coking  power  the  coal  may  possess.  For  coals  which  do  not  readily 
smoulder,  heat  in  a  muffle  furnace  from  cold  to  the  required 
temperature  at  a  rate  that  avoids  decrepitation.  Break  up  the  heaps,  if 
necessary,  and  complete  the  incineration  in  a  muffle  furnace  previously 
heated  to  the  required  temperature  After  incineration,  allow  the  ash  to 
cool  in  a  place  free  from  draughts.  When  cold,  transfer  to  a  tared  weigh- 
ing bottle  and  weigh,  removing  the  last  particles  with  a  brush.    Grind  the 


15 


IS  1 1355  *  1984 

ash  as  fine  as  possible,  mix  thoroughly  and  transfer  the  ash  to  an  air*tight 
specimen  tube.     Calculate  the  percentage  of  bulk  ash  in  the  dry  coal. 

6,4.1  For  coals,  a  temperature  of  550-600°C  provides  ash  which  is 
relatively  easily  dissolved.  For  high-temperature  cokes  a  temperature  of 
IIS^'C,  with  occasional  stirring  of  th.  mass  to  give  all  the  ash  access  to  air, 
is  necessary  to  avoid  too  protracted  an  incineration.  From  3  to  8  g  of  ash 
will  be  required  for  the  main  analysis.  The  moisture  content  must  be 
determined  on  a  separate  portion.  The  whole  of  the  ash  for  general 
analysis  may  be  prepared  by  the  standard  method  if  preferred.  No 
correlation  factor  I  see  5.4.3  (c)  ]  is  required  in  this  case  but  care  shall  be 
taken  to  ensure  that  moisture  and  carbon  dioxide  picked  up  during 
grinding  are  removed  by  incineration  for  30  minutes  at  815  +  lO'C  before 
weighing  out  ash  for  analysis 

6.5  Solution  of  Ash  and  Determination  of  Silica  and  Barium  Oxide 

6.5.1  Accurately  weigh  I'Oto  Tl  g  of  ash  {see  6.4)  in  a  platinum 
crucible  or  a  hard  glass  beaker.  Cover  the  ash  with  10  ml  of  concentrated 
hydrochloric  acid,  allow  to  digest  at  the  boiling  point— covering  the  crucible 
with  its  lid— and  continue  the  digestion  on  the  hot-air  bath  until  about  half 
the  liquid  has  been  evaporated.  Add  a  further  5  ml  of  the  acid  and  again 
digest  at  the  boiling  point  to  half  bulk.  Add  another  5  ml  of  concentrated 
hydrochloric  acid  and  continue  the  digestion  until  only  2  or  3  ml  of  liquid 
remain. 

6.5.2  Transfer  the  crucible  and  the  lid  to  a  platinum  basin,  containing 
73  to  100  ml  of  hot  water.  Turn  the  crucible  on  its  side  and  digest  at  the 
boiling  point  or  just  below  for  about  20  minutes,  protecting  the  liquid  from 
contamination  by  dust  in  this  and  subsequent  operations.  Remove  the 
crucible  and  lid,  wa«^h  them  clean  with  hot  water,  and  filter  the  hot  liquid 
through  a  fine,  low-ash,  filter  paper  in  to  a  platinum  basin.  Wash  the  residue 
five  times  with  hot  water,  collecting  the  washings  with  the  filtrate. 
Evaporate  on  a  water  bath. 

Note— Platinum  vessels  should  be  ust'd  to  preclude  contamination  by  silica  from 
glassware.  If  glassware  is  used  it  should  be  of  go«)d  quality  resistance  glass  and  the 
mside  surfaces  shou  d  be  free  from  scratches  or  chips  Blank  determinations  of  the 
silica  extracted  from  the  glass  under  he  conditions  of  the  method  must  be  made. 
Cover  glasses  are  usually  made  of  soft  glass  and  yield  a  little  soluble  silica. 

6.5.3  Transfer  the  wet  filter  paper  and  the  r<*sidue  to  a  platinum  crucible 
and,  after  gentle  heating,  incinerate  Mt  a  dull-red  heat.  Allow  to  cool  and 
mix  the  residue  thoroughly  in  the  crucible  with  4  g  of  anhydrous  sodium 
carbonate.  Cover  the  crucible  with  its  lid  and  heat  by  means  of  an  ordinary

burner  until  fusion  point  is  reached.  Raise  the  temperature  of  the  fused 
mass  to  about  1  OOO^C  at  a  rate  which  avoids  excessive  turbulence ,

of  a  platinum-iron  alloy  which  is  seen  as  a  black  stain  on  ignition, 
remove  by  alternate  ignition  and  extraction  with  concentrated  hydrochloric

6.5.4  Allow  the  crucible  to  cool,  then  heat  rapidly  to  about  400°C  and 
immediately  plunge  the  lower  two-thirds  of  the  crucible  into  cold  water  to

Cover  the  basin  and  slowly  add  15  ml  of  concentrated  hydrochloric  acid. 
Break  up  any  mass  of  silica  with  a  glass  rod.  Add  one  or  two  drops  of 
hydrogen  peroxide  to  decompose  any  manganic  acid  which  may  have  come 
from  manganates  formed  during  the  fusion.  Heat  the  liquid  gently  to 
boiling  point  and  remove  the  cover  glass,  washing  the  underside  into  the 
liquid.  Lift  out  the  crucible  and  lid  by  means  ol  a  thin  glass  rod,  washing 
each  into  the  liquid.  Clean  the  inside  of  the  crucible  with  water  and  a 
rubber  tipped  glass  rod,  adding  the  washings  to  the  liquid.  Add  10  ml  of 
ammonium  sulphate  solution. 

6.5.5  Transfer  the  liquid  and  precipitate  to  the  vessel  in  which  the  acid 
solution  of  the  ash  has  been  evaporating  (  see  6.5.2  ).  Evaporate  the  whole 
to  dryness  on  a  water-bath.  1  o  hasten  the  process,  break-up  occasionally 
the  crust  formed  on  the  solution  and  v,hcn  nearly  dry,  break-up  the  crystal

Cool,  cover  the  basin  and  add  10  ml  of  concentrated  hydrochloric  acid, 
followed,  after  two  to  thiee  minutes,  by  90  ml  of  hot  water.  Remove  the 
cover  glass,  washing  the  underside  into  the  liquid.  Heat  the  hquid  to 
boiling  point  and  maintain  it  at  the  boiling  point  for  10  minutes.  Decant 
the  supernatant  liquid  through  a  rapid,  lowash,  lilter  paper,  subsequently

three  times  with  hot  water.  Retain  the  residue.  Replace  the  washings  and 
filtrate  into  the  basin  used  for  evaporation  and  evaporate  to  dryness  on  a 
water-bath.  Transfer  the  covered  basin  to  an  oven  maintained  at  1  lO^C 
and  heat  for  one  hour. 

6.5.6  Cool,  cover  the  basin  and  add  5  ml  of  concentrated   hydrochloric 
acid  and  digest  on  a  water-bath  for  10  minutes.    Add  9o  ml  of  hot  water

and  remove  the  cover.  Allow  to  boil  gently  until  the  precipitate  is  white,

6.5.8  Moisten  the  ignited  residue  with  water  and  cautiously  add  three

hydrofluoric  acid  and  ignite  as  before.  Cool  in  a  desiccator  and  weigh. 
Repeat  the  second  acid  treatment  and  ignite  to  constant  mass.  The  total  loss 
in  mass  caused  by  the  acid  treatment  represents  the  amount  of  silica,  except 
for  traces  which  may  have  escaped  separation  and  which  are  recovered 
subsequently  (  see  6.7.2  ).

with  the  melt.  Continue  the  fusion  for  10  minutes.  Cool  and  dissolve 
me  melt  in  100  ml  of  boiling  water  containing  a  slight  excess  of  hydro- 
chloric acid.  Clean  the  crucible  with  a  rubber-tipped  glass  rod.  Add  5  ml 
of  ammonium  sulphate  solution.  If  a  white  precipitate  is  obtained  conti- 
nue boiling  for  5  minutes  and  allow  to  stand  for  4  hours  in  a  platinum 
basin.  Remove  precipitate  by  filtering  through  a  fine,  low-ash,  filter  paper 
or  through  asbestos  in  a  Gooch  crucible  and  determine  it  as  barium 
sulphate  in  the  normal  way.     Express  the  barium  as  barium  oxide. 

6.5.10  Add  the  filtrate  from  the  barium  separation,  or  the  solution 
of  the  melt,  if  this  is  clear,  to  the  filtrate  from  the  sihca  separation 
(  see  6.5.6  ). 

6.6  Recovery  of  Traces  of  Silica  and  Determination  of  Oxides  of  Iron 
Group 

6.6.1  To  the  combined  filtrates  and  washings  (  see  6.5,6  and  6.5.10  ) 
add  2  to   3  g  of  ammonium  chloride,  heat  to   incipient  boiling    and 

18 


IS  1 1355 -1984 

continuously  add  concentrated  ammonium  hydroxide  solution  drop  by  drop, 
stirring  briskly  with  a  rubber  tipped  glass  rod,  until  the  red  colour  of 
colloidal  ferric  hydroxide  is  seen.  Test  the  liquid  with  an  indicator  thread 
and  continue  to  add  ammonium  hydroxide  drop-wise  with  brisk  stirring 
until  the  liquid  is  just  alkaline.  If  an  excess  of  ammonium  hydroxide  is 
added  accidentally,  or  if  the  liquid  is  found  to  be  alkaline  on  first  testing, 
add  concentrated  hydrochloric  acid  drop  by  drop  until  one  drop  changes 
the  indicator  colour  to  pinkish-red.  Then  proceed  with  the  addition  of 
ammonium  hydroxide  dropwise. 

6.6.2  Raise  the  temperature  of  the  liquid  to  just  boiling,  remove  imme- 
diately from  the  source  of  heat  or  keep  the  covered  solution  at  a  lower 
temperature  for  5  to  10  minutes  and  then  allow  to  stand  at  room 
temperature  till  the  precipitate  has  settled.  Boiling  makes  the  precipitate 
slimy  which  settles  very  slowly.  Decani  the  supernatant  liquid  through  a 
rapid,  low-ash  filter  paper  and  transfer  the  precipitate  to  the  paper. 
Removal  of  the  last  traces  of  precipitate  is  not  necessary.  Wash  twice 
with  a  cold  solution  of  amn^onium  nitrate  and  then  twice  with  hot  water. 
After  the  last  washing  has  drained,  remove  the  beaker  containing  the 
filtrate  and  replace  the  beaker  used  in  the  precipitation  ( see  6.6.1  ), 
Evaporate  the  fihrate  to  50  to  100  ml  on  a  hot  plate. 

6.6.3  Push  a  hole  through  the  bottom  of  the  filter  paper  with  a  thin 
glass  rod  and  place  the  rod  in  the  beaker  below.  Wash  as  much 
as  possible  of  the  precipitate  to  the  beaker  using  the  minimum  quantity 
of  water  directed  in  a  strong  fine  jet.  Rinse  the  filter  paper  with  3-ni. 
portions  of  concentrated  hydrochloric  acid,  washing  with  hot  water 
and  each  rinsing,  until  the  paper  is  white.  Digest  the  acid  mixture  at 
incipient  boiling  until  the  precipitate  has  dissolved,  meanwhile  incinerate 
the  filter  paper  in  a  platinum  crucible  and  ndd  the  ash  to  the  acid 
solution.  Dilute  the  acid  mixture  to  about  300  ml  with  freshly  heat- 
ed water  and  repeat  the  precipitation  with  concentrated  ammonium 
hydroxide  solution  exactly  as  described  under  6,6,1  and  6.6.2.  Allow 
to  stand  only  as  long  as  is  necessary  for  settling. 

6.6.4  Decant  the  supernatant  liquid  through  a  rapid,  low-ash,  filter 
paper  and  transfer  the  precipitate  to  the  paper.  Complete  the 
transfer  of  the  precipitate  from  the  beaker  by  cleaning  the  inside  with 
about  3-ml  of  hot  water  to  which  one  drop  of  concentrated  hydrochloric 
acid  has  been  added,  using  a  rubber-tipped  glass  rod.  Wash  down  the 
sides  of  the  beaker  and  the  glass  rod,  add  one  drop  of  methyl  red  indi- 
cator and  make  just  alkaline  with  dilute  ammonium  hydroxide  solution. 
Transfer  the  whole  on  to  the  filter  paper.  Wash  the  total  precipitate 
five  times  with  ammonium  nitrate  solution  and  finally  three  tinfcs 
with  cold  water.  Drv  the  precipitate  and  paper  in  an  oven  at  100  to

6.6.5  Add  the  filtrate  and  washings  to  the  filtrato  obtained  under  6.6.2

6.9  Determination  of  Titanium  Dioxide  -  Detach  the  glass  bulb  from

air  may  be  displaced  from  the  tubing  by  pinching.  Close  the  clip  and  then 
the  tap,  and  pour  out  the  excess  water  in  the  tunnel.  Introduce  into  the 
funnel  100  ml  of  the  solution  of  the  iron  group  (  si'e  6.7.3  ),  40  ml  of  weak 
sulphuric  acid  and  20  ml  of  zinc  amalgam.  Add  one  tablet  of  sodium 
bicarbonate  and  immediately  i]\  the  uncorked  tube  in  the  top  of  ihe  funnel. 
As  soon  as  effervescence  has  ceased,  add  the  broken  poitii^ns  of  another 
bicarbonate  tablet  down  the  glass  tube.  When  efl^ervescence  is  just 
ceasing,  fit  the  cork  to  the  top  of  the  glass  tube.  Shake  the  apparatus 
vigorously  for  10  to  15  minutes.  This  is  the  most  important  part  of  the 
determination.  It  is  essential  that  the  apparatus  should  be  shaken  suffici- 
ently vigi)rously  to  throw  the  amalgam  up  into  the  aqueous  layer-swirling 
moiion  is  useless.  Ease  the  top  cork  a  little,  every  two  minutes,  to 
release  ex^e^s  pressure.  Replace  the  apparatus  in  a  stand.  Fill  a  burette 
with  0"02  N  solution  of  ferric  sulphate.  Open  the  spring  clip  (  the 
apparatus  remains  closed  to  the  air  )  and  then  the  tap  of  the  funnel.  By 
alternitely  pinching  and  releasing  the  rubber  tubing,  make  the  amalgan 
drop  into  the  hulb,  air-free  water  being  displaced.  Close  the  funnel  tap 
as  the  last  of  the  amalgam  passes  through  and  detach  the  bulb  and  the 
spring  clip.  Uncork  the  top  glass  tube  and  pour  5  ml  of  potassium 
thiocyanatc  solution  down  the  tube.    Remove  the  tube  and  the  bung,  and

6.10  Estimation  of  Alumina  —  The  amount  of  phosphate  in  the  ash  is 
determined  on  a  separate  portion  of  ash  as  described  under  6.15.  If  this 
amount,  together  with  the  amounts  of  silica  (  see  6.7.2 ),  ferric  oxide 
(  see  6.8  ),  titania  (  see  6.9  ),  is  deduced  from  the  total  mass  of  oxides 
(  see  6.6.6  ),  the  amount  of  alumina  may  be  calculated. 

6.11  Separation  of  Platinum  and  Manganese 

6.11.1  Adjust  the  filtrate  from  the  separation  of  the  iron  group  ( see  6.6.5 ) 
to  about  300  ml  by  evaporation  or  dilution  with  water  as  necessary.  Add 
3  ml  of  concentrated  hydrochloric  acid  and  heat  to  incipient  boiling.  Pass 
through  the  liqud  a  stream  of  hydrogen  sulphide  at  the  rate  of  5  to  10 
bubbles  per  second  for  20  minutes,  while  maintaining  this  temperature. 
Filter  the  solution  hot  through  a  fine  filter  paper  and  wash  the  precipitate 
four  times  with  water  containing  hydrogen  sulphide.  Incinerate  the  filter 
paper  and  precipiiate  in  a  platinum,  silica  or  porcelain  crucible  by  gently 
heatifjg,  burning  off  the  last  traces  of  carbon  at  about  800X.  Treat  the 
residue  with  2  ml  of  boiling,  concentrated  hydrochloric  acid,  dilute  to  10  ml 
and  filter  through  a  fine  filter  paper  into  the  main  filtrate.  Discard  the 
precipitate  which  is  due  to  platinum  contributed  by  the  laboratory 
apparatus. 

6J1.2  Cool  the  combined  filtrates  to  room  temperature  and  add  6  ml 
of  concentrated  ammonium  hydroxide  solution.  Transfer  the  liquid  to  a 
flask  just  large  enough  to  contain  it  and  pass  hydrogen  sulphide  at  the 
rate  of  5  to  10  bubbles  per  second  for  10  minutes.  Add  2  ml  of  concentrated 
ammonium  hydroxide  solution,  cork  the  flask  and  allow  to  stand  overnight. 
Filter  the  liquid  through  a  fine  filter  paper,  washing  the  precipitate  four 
times  with  water  containing  a  trace  of  ammonium  chloride  and  hydrogen 
sulphide.    Discard  the  precipitate  which  is  due  to  manganese. 

6.11.3  Add  a  slight  excess  of  concentrated  hydrochloric  acid  to  the 
filtrate  and  boil  until  there  is  no  smell  of  hydrogen  sulphide.  Add  10  ml 
of  bromine  wator  and  boil  until  the  bromine  colour  has  gone.  If  a 
precipitate  is  formed,  filter  and  extract  the  residue  as  previously  described 
under  6.11.1.  Discard  the  precipitate.  The  filtrate  is  in  a  suitable  state  for 
the  determination  of  calcium  oxide  (  see  6.12  ). 

6.12  Determination  of  Calcium  Oxide 

6.12.1  Heat  the  filtrate  obtained  in  641.3  to  boiling  and,  whilst  stirring, 
add  40  ml  of  hot  saturated  ammonium  oxalate  solution  followed  by 

22 


IS  1 1355  -  19^ 

concentrated  ammonium  hydroxide  solution  drop  by  drop  until  there  is  an 
excess.  Continue  boiling  for  5  to  10  minutes  and  allow  to  stand  for'a 
minimum  period  of  four  hours,  or  until  the  precipitate  has  settled 
completely.  Decant  the  clear  liquid  through  a  fine  filter  paper  without 
transferring  the  precipitate.  Remove  the  beaker  containing  the  filtrate  and 
replace  with  the  one  containing  precipitate.     Reserve  the  filtrate. 

6.12.2  Wash  the  filter  paper  five  times  with  10  ml  of  hot,  dilute, 
hydrochloric  acid  followed  by  one  washing  with  water.  Dilute  the 
solution  to  300  ml,  boil  and  add  5  ml  of  hot  saturated  ammonium  oxalate 
solution  and  a  slight  excess  of  ammonium  hydroxide,  stirring  during 
the  additions.  Allow  to  stand  for  a  minimum  period  of  four  hours  as 
under  6.12.1. 

6.12.3  Filter  the  liquid  through  a  fine  filter  paper  or  preferably  through 
asbestos  in  a  Gooch  crucible.  Transfer  the  precipitate  to  the  filter,  wash 
five  times  with  dilute  ammonium  oxalate  solution  and  then  five  times 
with  5-ml  portions  of  warm  water.  Combine  the  filtrate  and  washing  with 
those  under  6.12.1  and  reserve. 

Note  —  Asbestos  in  a  Gooch  crucible  with  a  detachable  base  is  the  best  filtering 
medium.  It  is  quicker  than  filter  paper  and  the  washing  of  precipitate  is  more  thorough. 

6.12.4  Transfer  the  precipitate  into  a  beaker  using  100  ml  of  warm,  weak 
sulphuric  acid.  If  asbestos  has  been  used,  transfer  the  whole  contents  of 
the  crucible  to  the  beaker;  if  filter  paper  has  been  used  make  a  small  hole 
in  the  apex  of  the  cone  with  a  thin  glass  rod  and  rinse  the  precipitate  into 
the  beaker  with  the  sulphuric  acid.  Warm  the  solution  to  about  70°C  and 
titrate  with  a  dccinormal  solution  of  potassium  permanganate.  If  filter 
paper  has  been  used,  drop  the  paper  into  the  solution  and  complete  the 
titration.  Calculate  on  the  basis  that  1  ml  of  decinormal  solution  of 
potassium  permanganate  is  equivalent  to  0002  804  g  of  calcium  oxide 
i  CaO  ) 

6.13  Determiiuition  of  Magnesium  Oxide 

6.13.1  Acidify  the  combined  filtrates  reserved  in  6.12.3  by  the  addition

tipped  glass  rod,  taking  care  that  it  does  not  touch  the  sides.  Whilst 
stirring,  add  an  excess  of  sodium  phosphate  solution  followed  by  an 
amount  of  concentrated  ammonium  hydroxide  solution  equal  to  one-fifth 
of  the  volume  of  the  solution.  Allow  the  liquid  to  stand  overnight. 

6.13.2  Filter    through    a   fine    filter  paper    without  trans   fining    the 
precipitate.    Discard  the  filtrate  and  replace  with  the  beaker  used  in  the 
precipitation.    Wash  the  filter  paper  five  times  with  hot,  dilute  hydrochlo- 
ric acid.  Dilute  the  solution  to  200  ml  and  re-precipitate   but   using  only

6.14  Determination  of  Oxide  of  Manganese  —  Boil  one  gram  of  ash  accu- 
rately weighed,  with  15  ml  of  sulphuric  acid  (  1:1  )  for  5  minutes,  allow  to

continuous  agitation.  Add  50  ml  of  weak  nitric  acid,  and  filter  through 
a  thin  layer  of  asbestos  using  a  Hirsch  funnel.  Wash  with  80  ml  of  weak 
nitric  acid.  Discard  the  residue.  Add  a  measured  excess  of  a  decinormal 
solution  of  ferrous  ammonium  sulphate  to  the  combined  filtrate  za6 
washings  and  titrate  the  excess  ferrous  iron  present  with  potassium  per- 
manganate solution.  Calculate  on  the  basis  that  0*001  525  g  of  the 
oxide  of  manganese  (  Mn,04 )  is  equivalent  to  1  ml  of  decinormal  ferrous 
ammonium  sulphate  solution. 

6.15  Phosphorus  In  Ash  of  Coal  and  Coke 

6.15.0  General  —  Besides  carbon,  hydrogen,  nitrogen  and  sulphur,  which 
occur  in  all  coals  and  cokes  in  appreciable  quantities,  it  is  sometimes 
necessary  also  to  determine  the  percentage  of  phosphorus,  chlorine  and 
arsenic  which  are  present  in  smaller  quantities.  The  determina'ion  for 
chlorine  and  arsenic  are  made  on  the  material  taken  from  the  analysis 
sample  of  0'5  kg  of  air-dried  coal  groimd  to  pass  IS  Sieve  20  (  21 1  microns  ). 
The  phosphorus  is  usually  determined  in  the  ash. 

6.15.1  General  Outline 

a)    There  are  two  methods,   one  gravimetric  (  phosphomolybdate ) 
and  the  other  volumetric.    In  the  gravimetric  method   a  known 

24 


I« 


IS  t  1355  .  1984 

mass  of  the  ash  is  heated  with  a  mixture  of  hydrofluoric 
and  nitric  acids  to  remove  silica  which  escapes  as  silicon 
tetrafluoride.  Alternatively,  a  known  mass  of  thj  ash  is  fused 
with  a  mixture  of  potassium  and  sodium  carbonate.  The 
fused  mass  is  extracted  with  dilute  nitric  acid  and  the  silica 
removed  by  fiUering. 

b)  The  phosphoric  acid  in  the  aqueous  extract  is  precipitated  as 
phosphomolybdate  which  is  then  weighed  to  determine  the 
percentage  by  mass  of  phosphorus.  From  the  value  of  ash 
determined  as  prescribed  under  «  of  IS  :  !35()^(  Part  I  )  -  1969" 
the  results  now  obtained,  the  percentage  of  phosphorous  in  the 
air-dried  prepiircd  sample  is  calculated. 

c)  Errors  due  to  the  presence  of  arsenic  in  the  amounts  normally 
present  in  coal  are  insignificant.  The  inhibiting  effect  of  tita- 
nium is  reduced  lo  negligible  proportions  by  the  strength  of 
the  nitric  acid  used.  In  the  cases  where  the  interference  due  to 
arsenic  is  believed  to  be  significant,  the  following  precautions 
may  be  taken  : 

1)  The  coal  ash  may  be  digested  with  a  mixture  containing 
ferric  chloride,  hydrochloric  acid  and  hydrogen  bromide  to 
expel  the  arsenic  as  the  volatile  arsenious  chloride. 

2)  The  phosphomolybdate  precipitation  may  be  carried  out  at 
50X.

The  combined  volume  of  the  washings  and  the  original 
solution  should  be  about  80  ml.  Cover  the  beaker  with  a 
clock  glass  and  boil  the  contents  of  the  beaker  for  1 5 
minutes,  allowing  a  glass  rod  to  stand  in  it  to  inhibit 
bumping.

phosphomolybdatc  precipitate  ( in  the  beaker  )  in  10  ml

6.16  Determination  of  Alkalis 

6.16.1  Important  Precaution  —  It  is  extremely  important  that  specially 
prepared  reagents,  as  free  as  possible,  from  alkali  metals  should  be 
used. 

6.16.2  Mix  0*8  g  of  bulk  ash  (  see  5.4.3  ),  accurately  weighed,  with  0*8  g 
of  ammonium  chloride  and  6  g  of  precipitated  calcium  carbonate  by  grind- 
ing together  in  an  agate  mortar.  Transfer  the  mixture  to  a  platinum 
crucible  fitted  with  a  lid,  a  little  calcium  carbonate  having  been  placed 
previously  at  the  bottom  of  the  crucible.  Place  the  crucible  in  a  suit- 
able shield  of  asbestos-cement  board  so  arranged  that  only  the  lower 
half  of  the  crucible  is  directly  heated.  Heat  gently  until  ammonia  ceases  to 
be  evolved,  then  raise  the  temperature  to  about  7C0'  C  (  dull-red  heat ), 
maintaining  at  this  temperature  for  75  minutes. 

6.16.3  Slake  the  cooled  sintered  mass  with  about  5  ml  of  water, 
transfer  the  contents  of  the  crucible  to  a  beaker  and  digest  with  50  ml 
of  hot  water.  Allow  to  settle  and  decant  the  supernatant  liquid 
through  a  fine  filter  paper.  Repeat  the  digestion  and  decantation  twice, 
finally  transferring  the  residue  to  the  filter  paper.  Wash  with  hot 
water.   Discard  the  residue. 

29 


IS  1 1355  -  1984 

6.16.4  Precipitate  any  sulphate  present  in  the  combined  filtrates  by 
the  addition,  in  the  normal  manner,  of  barium  chloride  solution, 
slightly  acidified  with  hydrochloiic  acid.  Filter  through  a  fine  filter 
paper  and  discard  the  residue. 

6.16.5  Treat  the  filtcrate  successively  with  slight  excesses  of  both 
concentrated  ammonium  hydroxide  solution  and  ammonium  carbonate 
solution.  Filter  through  a  line  filter  paper,  rcdissolvt  the  precipitate  in 
dilute  h>drochloric  acid,  and  repeat  the  precipitation  and  filtration. 
Discard  the  residue.  Evaporate  the  combined  filtrate  to  dryness  in  a 
platinum  basin  and  remove  ammonium  salts  by  careful  baking  in  a 
muflUe  furnace  at  450''C. 

6.16.6  Rinse  down  the  sides  of  the  basin  with  25  ml  of  hot  water. 
Add  dilute  barium  chloride  solution  drop  by  drop,  until  one  drop 
causes  no  further  precipitation.  Add  1  ml  of  dilute  ammonium  oxalate 
solution,  followed  by  2  ml  of  ammonium  carbonate  solution  and  one 
drop  of  concentrated  ammonium  hydroxide  solution.  Allow  the  mixture 
to  stand  for  at  least  4  hours,  preferably  overnight. 

6.16.7  Filter  through  a  small,  fine,  filter  paper  into  a  platinum  basin 
washing  the  precipitate  three  times  with  water.  Discard  the  precipitate. 
Fvaporate  the  filtrate  to  dryness  and  remove  the  ammonium  salts  as 
described   under   6.16.S.   Extract  the   baked   residue   with   5  to  10  ml  of 

hot  water  and  filter  through  a  small,  fine,  filter  paper  into  a  weighed 
platinum  basin,  washing  the  paper  six  times  with  hot  water.  Discard  the 
residue.  Add  10  drops  of  concentrated  hydrochloric  acid  to  the  filtrate 
and  evaporate  the  mixture  to  dryness.  Heat  in  a  muffle  furnace  at  450*^0. 
Cool  in  a  desiccator  and  rewcigh.  The  increase  in  the  mass  is  the  mass 
of  mixed  alkali  chlorides  present. 

6.16.8  Dissolve  the  mixed  chlorides  in  about  5  ml  of  water  and  trans- 
fer to  a  small  evaporating  basin  of  good  quality  glass.  Add  2  ml 
of  perchloric  acid  (  see  5.5.3  )  and  gently  evaporate  to  dryness  on  a  hot 
plate  which  is  not  above  350^C.  Cool,  add  5  ml  of  water  and  evaporate 
to  dryness  as  before. 

6.16.9  Dry  a  50-ml  conical  flask  and  a  filter  stick  and  weigh  together. 
Remove  the  filter  stick  temporarily  to  a  desiccator  or  stoppered  tube. 
Transfer  the  dried  residue  from  the  evaporating  basin  to  the  conical  flask 
by  successive  rinsings  with  2  ml  of  hot  water.  Evaporate  to  dryness  in  the 
flask,  finishing  in  an  oven  for  one  hour  at  about  110°C.  Cool  in  a  desiccator. 
Add  3  ml  of  pure  ethyl  acetate  or  absolute  alcohol  saturated  with 
potassium  perchlorate,  cork  the  flask  ard  swirl  the  Hquids  around  gently 
for  5  minutes.  Remove  the  cork,  connect  the  filter  stick  to  a  suction  pump 
and  insert  it  into  the  solution.  Insert  a  strap  between  the  filter  stick  and 
the  pump   to  catch  the   filtrate.  Take  as  much  as  possible  of  the  solution 

30 


IS  1 1355  *  1984 

through  the  filter  stick.  Wash  down  the  inside  of  the  flask  and  the  outside 
of  the  filter  stick  with  four  separate  portions  of  5  ml  of  eihyl  acetate,  with 
drawing  each  separate  portions  through  the  filter  stick.  With  suction'  still 
applied^  immerse  the  lower  portion  of  the  flask  in  hot  water  and  draw  out 
the  vapour  of  ethyl  acetate.  Detach  the  filter  stick  and  again  dry  the  flask 
and  stick  at  110**C  to  constant  mass. 

6.16.10  Calculation  —  The  increase  in  mass  is  potassium  perchlorate. 
For  extreme  accuracy  and  to  correct  fc  r  the  amount  dissolved  by  the  ethyl 
acetate,  add  0*000  3  g  to  the  mass  of  potassium  perchlorate  found. 
Calculate  the  alkali  content  on  the  following  basis: 

a)  1  g  of  potassium  perchlorate  is  equivalent  to  0538  1  g  of 
potassium  chloride  (  KCl ), 

b)  1  g  of  potassium  chloride  is  equivalent  to  0'631  4  g  of  potassium 
oxide  (  K2O  ),  and 

c)  1  g  of  sodium  chloride  i  s  equivalent  to  0*530  g  of  sodium  oxide 
(Na,0). 

6.17  Determination  of  Sulphur 

6.17.0  The  determination  of  sulphur  (  as  trioxide  )  shall  be  carried  out 
on  standard  ash, 

6.17.1  Treat  an  accurately-known  mass  {  usually  about  0*5  g  )  of  standard 
ash  with  5  ml  of  bromine  water  and  100  ml  of  dilute  hydrochloric  acid 
and  boil  for  one  hour.  Filter  through  a  fine  filter  paper  and  wash  the 
insoluble  residue  with  hot  water.  Reserve  the  residue.  Neutralize  the 
filtrate  with  concentrated  ammonium  hydroxide  solution  and  add  2  ml  of 
concentrated  hydrochloric  acid.  Make  up  the  volume  to  about  250  mJ. 
Boil  the  solution,  and,  while  boiling,  treat  it  with  1 5  ml  of  concentrated 
barium  chloride  solution,  added  drop  by  drop,  to  permit  uninterrupted 
boiling.  Continue  boiling  for  a  further  15  minutes  and  allow  to  stand  for  a 
minimum  period  of  4  hours  in  a  sulphur-free  atmosphere  and  protected 
from  dust. 

6.17.2. Filter,  using  one  of  the  following  techniques: 

a)  By  gravity,  through  an  ashless  fine-textured  double  acid-waihed 
filter  paper  in  a  fluted,  long-stemmed,  60°  funnel,  the  filter- 
circle  being  carefully  folded  to  fit  the  funnel  so  that  the  item 
remains  full  of  liquid. 

or 

b)  By  gravity,  through  a  filter-paper  pad  prepared  from  ashless 
double  acid-washed  filter  paper  (  see  Note  ). 

31 


IS  2  1355  - 1984 

Note  —  For  preparing  the  fihcr-papcr  pad.  shake  double  acid-washed 
filter-paper  clippings,  in  pieces  of  approximately  ]  sq  cm  area,  with  distilled 
water  in  a  bottle  until  the  paper  is  thoroughly  disintegrated.  Place  a  25  mm 
porcelain  filter  cone  in  a  75-mm  funnel  close  the  stem  of  the  funnel  wiih  a

\e\c\  it  with  a  flat-ended  glass  rod.  Allow  the  excess  water  to  drain  away  by

edges  with  the  glass  rod  as  drain  age  ceases.  Wash  finally  with  distilled

or 

c)     Under  suction,  using  good  quality  asbestos  in  a   Gooch  crucible 
which  has  been  dried  for  one  hour  at  130±I0''C  and  weighed. 

6.17.3  Wash  the  filter  with  hot  distilled  water,  using  not  more  than  250 
ml,  until  20  ml  ol  the  washings  give  not  more  than  a  faint  opalescence  with 
silver  nitrate  solution.  Place  wet  tiltcr  paper  in  an  ignited  and  weighed  silica 
or  platinum  capsule  on  a  silica  plate  and  insert  into  the  muffle  furnace  for  15 
minutes  at  800  ±  25'C.  If  a  filter  pad  is  used,  transfer  the  pad  to  the 
silica  capsule,  wipe  the  funnel  successively  with  two  halves  of  a  circle  of 
ashless  filter  paper  and  inciiierate  these  with  the  pad.  If  a  Gooch  crucible  is 
used,  dry  it  for  one  hour  at  130  ±  10X\  Cool  and  weigh. 

6.17.3.1  Ignition  is  achieved  rapidly  with  wet  paper  or  pad  and 
mechanical  loss  is  avoided  by  the  use  of  thick  silica  plate.  If  filter  paper 
is  used,  the  ignited  residue  shall  be  oxidized  by  the  addition  of  a  few  drops 
of  concentrated  sulphuric  acid  and  again  heated  and  cooled  before  weighing, 
but  this  is  seldom  necessary. 

6.17.4  Carry  out  a  blank  determinations  under  the  same  conditions  but 
omitting  the  coal-ash.  Pipette  10  ml  of  the  potassium  sulphate  solution  to 
the  filtrate  after  extraction.  Deduct  the  mass  of  the  barium  sulphate  found 
in  the  blank  determination,  less  the  barium  sulphate  equivalent  of  the 
potassium  sulphate  added,  from  the  mass  obtained  in  full  determination. 

6.17.5  One  gram  of  barium  sulphate  is  equivalent  to  0*343  1  g  of 
sulphur  trioxide  (SO3).  If  the  sulphur  trioxide content  is  loss  than  5  percent, 
the  determination  may  be  considered  to  be  concluded.  Jf  it  is  higher  than  5 
percent,  transfer  the  filter  paper  and  the  residue  (  sec  6.17.1  )  to  a  platinum 
crucible  and  burn  off  the  paper  by  smouldering  finally  removing  the 
residual  carbon  at  a  bright-red  heat.  Allow  to  cool  and  add  5  drops  of 
concentrated  nitric  acid  followed  by  10  drops  of  hydrofluoric  acid.  Place 
the  lid  on  the  crucible  and  heat  gently  to  drive  off  the  acid.  Slowly  raise 
the  temperature  to  800"C  and  allow  to  cool.  Repeate  the  acid  treatment 
using  5  drops  of  each  acid. 

6.17.6  To  the  cooled  residue  add  1  g  of  sodium  carbonate  and  heat  to 
fusion  for  about  30  minutes.  Dissolve  the  melt  in  100  ml  of  boiling  water 
containing  a  slight  excess  of  hydrochloric  acid.     Filter  through  a  fine  filter 

32

paper.  Discard  the  residue.  Determine  the  sulphate  present  in  the  filtrate 
by  precipitalion  vvjih  barium  chloride  as  previously  described.  Add  the 
amount  of  sulphate  to  that  already  obtained  to  account  Tor  the  total 
sulphate  present.

7.3  Preparation  of  Ash  —  The  ash  is  prepared  as  described  under  6.3 
or  6.4.  For  complete  analysis  in  duplicate  ">  to  8  g  of  bulk  ash  are  required. 
The  ash  as  made  under  6.4  absorbs  moisture  and  carbon  dioxide  during 
grinding.  Before  carrying  out  the  analysis,  the  ground  ash  is  therefore 
heated  in  a  silica  dish  at  a  temperature  of  815  ±  1  S^C  for  about  30 
minutes.   Analysis  should  be  carried  out  in  duplicate. 

7.4  Procedure 

7.4.1  The  first  stage  covers  the  fusion  of  ash  with  sodium  carbonate; 
the  method  for  ash  low  in  iron  content  is  different  from  the  method  for 
ash  high  in  iron  content : 

a)  For  ash  low  in  iron  —  Accurately  weigh  about  0'5  g  of  ash  in 
a  platinum  crucible  and  mix  thoroughly  with  3  g  of  sodium 
carbonate  using  a  clean  glass  rod.  Brush  into  the  crucible  with 
a  camel  hair  brush  any  particles  adhering  to  the  rod.  Sprinkle 
one  gram  of  sodium  carbonate  over  the  mixture  and  fuse  as 
described  under  7.4.1(c). 

b)  For  ash  high  in  iron  —  If  the  ash  contains  much  iron,  as  will 
be  evident  from  the  colour,  extraction  with  concentrated  hydro- 
chloric acid  should  precede  the  fusion  of  the  residue.  For 
this  digest  about  0'5  g  oftheish,  accurately  weighed,  with  10 
ml  of  concentrated  hydrochloric  acid  in  a  porcelain  basin, 
fitted  with  a  cover- glass,  on  a  steam-bath  until  only  half  the 
acid  remains.  Repeat  the  operation  with  a  further  5-ml 
portion  of  acid.  Digeit  the  mass  with  about  50-ml  of  hot  water 
for  about  1 5  minutes.  Filter  through  a  filter  paper  {  Whatman 
No.  42  )  into  a  porcelain  basin.  Wash  the  residue  5  to  6  times 
with  hot  water,  collecting  tiie  washings  with  the  main  filtrate. 
Reserve  the  filtrate  [  see  7.4.2(a)  ].  Transfer  the  residue  with 
its  filter  paper  to  a  platinum  crucible  and  dry  with  slow  heat. 
Finally,  incinerate  at  a  dull-red  heat  to  remove  carbonaceous

placing  the  lid  across  the  width  of  the  crucible.  Mix  ihe  non- 
carbonaceous  residue  with  3  g  of  sodium  carbonate  as  described 
in  7.4J<a)  and  fuse  as  described  under  7.4.1(c). 

c)  Fusion  —  Cover  the  crucible  with  the  lid  and  raise  the  heat 
slowly.  After  a  few  minutes,  raise  the  temperature  until  fusion 
takes  p  ace.  Maintain  fusion  for  about  half  an  hour,  care 
being  t  iken  to  prevent  boiling  of  excessive  turbulence  of  the

Evaporate  the  filtrate  again  on  a  water-bath  and,  when  dry, 
grind  the  mass  with  a  glass  rod  and  then  place  in  the 
air-oven  for  two  hours,  grinding  the  mass  once  more  during 
this  heating.  Remove  the  basin  and  allow  it  to  cool.  When

7.4.3  Determination  of  Barium  Oxide  —  Fuse  the  residue  in  the  platinum 
crucible  with  0*5  g  of  sodium  carbonate.  Cool,  and  dissolve,  the  melt  in

is  due  to  barium  sulphate.  Digest  the  precipitate  for  at  further  15 
minutes,  allow  it  to  stand  for  30  minutes,  and  then  filler  through  a  fine 
textured  double  acid-washed  filter  paper  (  Whatman  No.  42  )  and  keep  the 
filtrate.  Wash  the  precipitate  i\\'c  to  six  times  with  hot  water,  ignite  the 
pr-cipitate  of  barium  sulphate  in  the  usual  manner  (  see  6.17  )  and  weigh 
tiic  barium  sulphate.  Report  the  result  as  percentage  of  barium  oxide 
\  BaO  ). 

7.4.4  Precipitation  of  Mixed  Oxides 

a)  Add  the  filtrate  from  silica  separation  [  see  7.4.2(b)  ].  Evaporate

boiling  solution  add  two  drops  of  methyl  red  indicator.  In  case 
much  iron  is  present  (  as  judged  from  the  colour  of  the  solution  ) 
additions  of  the  indicator  is  not  necessary.  Add  5  g  of 
ammonium  chloride  followed  by  concentrited  ammonium 
hydroxide  solution  with  continuous  stirring  with  a  glass  rod 
until  a  precipitate  just  appears.  Add  dilute  ammonium  hydro- 
xide solution  dropwise  and  test  with  methyl  red  indicator  thread 
until  the  solution  is  just  alk  «line.  Raise  the  temperature  of  the 
liquid  to  just  bi)iling,  remove  immediately  from  the  source  of 
heat  or  keep  the  covered  solution  at  a  lower  temperature  for  5 
to  10  minutes  and  then  allow  to  stand  at  room  temperature  until

taking  care  to  note  that  no  black  mass  results.  Cool  and 
weigh. 

c)  Calculate  on  the  basis  that  1  g  of  magnesium  pyrophosphate 
corresponds  to  0'362  1  g  of  magnesium  oxide  (MgO).

7.4.10  Determination  of  Alkalis 

a)  Spread  a  thin  layer  of  calcium  carbonate  at  the  bottom  of  a 
Lawrence  Smith  crucible.  Weigh  about  0*8  g  of  finely  ground 
bulk  ash  and  mix  with  0*8  g  of  ammonium  chloride  and  6*4  g 
of  precipitated  calcium  carbonate  by  grinding  together  in  an 
agate  mortar.  Carefully  transfer  the  whole  of  the  ground 
mixture  to  the  Lawrence  Smith  crucible.  Rinse  the  agate  mortar 
with  some  more  calcium  carbonate  and  traosFer  into  the  crucible. 
Cover  the  mixture  with  a  thin  layer  of  calcium  carbonate.  Place 
the  crucible  through  a  hole  in  an  asbestos  pad,  so  that  one- 
third  of  the  crucible  projects  below  the  pad.  Heat  the  crucible 
slowly  with  a  small  flame  until  odour  of  ammonia  is  no  longer 
perceptible.  In  case,  ammonium  chloride  sublimes  out,  slow 
down  the  rate  of  heating.  Then  heat  the  crucible  for  about  43 
minutes  in  such  a  way  that  the  lower  portion  of  the  crucible  is 
at  a  dull-red  heat. 

b)  Allow  to  cool,  rinse  the  lid,  and  add  15  ml  of  hot  water  and 
digest  in  a  steam  bath  for  10  minutes.  Transfer  the  contents 
into  a  large  agate  mortar  and  crush  the  lumps.  TYansfer  again 
into  a  porcelain  basin  or  preferably  a  platinum  basin.  Wash  the 
agate  mortar  several  times  to  remove  any  residual  particles,  and 
sufficient  water  to  the  basin  and  digest  for  about  half  an  hour. 
Filter  through  a  rapid,  low-ash  filter  paper  ( Whatman  No.  40  ) 
into  a  beaker. 

c)  Wash  the  residue  several  times  with  hot  water.  Take  the  residue 
in  the  basin  again  and^digest  for  half  an  hour  and  filter.  Repeat 
this  operation  3  to  4  times  depending  on  the  alkali  content. 
Combine  the  filtrates.  Add  sufficient  quantity  of  ammonium 
carbonate  solution  followed  by  dilute  ammonium  hydroxide 
solution  to  precipitate  the  calcium.  After  the  precipitate  has 
settled  filter.  Wash  the  precipitate  4  or  5  times  with  hot  water 
and  dissolve  in  minimum  quantity  of  diluta  hydrochloric  acid, 
and  precipitate  calcium  as  before.  Filter  again  and  combine  the 
filtrates.

and  then  decompose  the  ammonium  salts  tn  &  muffle  furnace

to  precipitate  any  sulphate.  Then  add  a  few  millilitres  of 
ammonium  oxalate  solution  and  2  to  3  drops  of  concentrated 
ammonium  hydroxide  solution.  Stand  for  6  hours  o'  preferably

overnight.  Filter  through  a  rapid,  low-ash  filter  paper 
(  Whatman  No.  40  )  into  a  tared  platinum  basin  and  wash  the 
residue  with  hot  water.  Evaporate  the  filtrate  and  washings  to

e)  Carry  out  a  blank  determination  with  appropriate  quantities  of
